Somehow Dune: Part Two managed to be even longer, louder, and somehow still feel like nothing was happening. In the first film, Paul Atreides was treated like a legendary figure before I ever understood why I should care about him. Unfortunately, Part Two doubles down on that. Everyone keeps looking at Paul like he’s the greatest thing to ever walk across the desert, but the movie never really earns that feeling. We’re constantly told he’s a messiah or the chosen one but I’m still waiting for the part where I understand why. Instead of watching a character become extraordinary, it feels like watching everyone else convince themselves that he already is. The Fremen’s devotion to Paul also made the story harder to take seriously. It feels less like a believable movement and more like an entire population suddenly joining a religion because the script told them to. And the final was strangely underwhelming. A story that spends so much time preparing for greatness somehow ends on a very ordinary note. Two movies, almost five hours, and my main takeaway is still: more sand, more silence, more people telling me Paul is special.

I think this is the greatest example of a “good” movie vs. an “enjoyable/favorite” movie I’ve ever seen. I say that because this movie is GREAT from nearly all technical standpoints. Great actors doing some great acting, absolutely beautiful cinematography and special effects, insanely impressive sets, and just a sheer feeling of grandness that, I feel, is only topped by a handful of movies. All around, just a beautifully made film. Still, I didn’t enjoy myself AT ALL. I don’t think the story is nearly as impressive as the first one, or impressive at all for that matter. I find it boring, confusing, and just honestly dull. I find that they waste unreasonable amounts of time on storylines that don’t matter and/or just aren’t entertaining, and rush the very few things I actually enjoyed. I mean, and this is obviously the card they were dealt, seeing as this was based on a book, it’s all just talking and politics, but they do it so different in this land, “Arakkis,” that half the film is spent explaining all of that through boring exposition and whatnot, and the other half is not very interesting at all, as someone who enjoys stories similar to this, like Game of Thrones. The action scenes, though VERY far and few were, again, gorgeously and impressively shot, but I feel lack stakes, substance, and, again, enjoyment. Half of the scenes just felt like Neo and Agent Smith going at it, even though Neo already knows all of the moves Agent Smith will make. This was a dumb comparison, in hindsight, but what I mean to say is that they’re un-compelling and boring for the most part, besides that gladiator-type fight in the middle and the fight scene with the big tank thing near the 40-minute mark. The characters- don’t get me started on the characters. I’m guessing this is something most people actually LIKE about Dune- seeing as they are able as realistic of characters you can write given their positions, but I sincerely couldn’t name you one that I care about/ like. I mean, in the first one, I cared about Paul because he actually had a personality, I liked Jason Momoa’s character a lot, and I thought the Baron was a very intriguing villain, but this time around, there was none of that charm. Everyone was just this boring, dull, character with seemingly the same personality, unless you’re Paul or his mother, because then you have NO personality, making the finale and all of the stuff with Chani pretty uninteresting and unrewarding to be quite honest. Again; the fact that this movie even got to be made is a wonder within itself- with all of those spacecrafts, settings, character designs, buildings, etc, that they had to create, shoot, and put to film is such a tasteful way, but I just didn’t enjoy it at all. I found it to be INSANELY long, like, blood-curdlingly long in my opinion, to the point where I was just actually started to breathe heavier (coming from someone who likes longer movies) and (with zero exaggeration whatsoever) probably checked how much longer it was roughly 15-20 times, very boring and dull, lifeless if you will, and everything I “liked” about it wasn’t done any better than what I’ve seen a gazillion times before. My rating: 3.4/10

I watched this movie right when it came out because I’m friends with this nerd who loves Dune. He’s read the books and everything, the books actually lose the plot after like the 3rd one according to him. For example the grandson of Paul (who is the main character further down the line) is actually just one of those sand worms, no human part he’s a sand worm and somehow that works I suppose. Anyways why did I give this a 2? Well there’s a few reasons. First I should mention I slammed 2 Four Lokos during the runtime of this movie, which got me pretty loko ngl. In fact I blacked out at some point during the film and spawned back in at the final fight. But before that happened I felt the movie was too slow and convoluted. My very informed opinion was backed up because my friend said the books do a much better job of explaining what’s going on and it’s hard to explain it visually which is what the movie has to do. Also he had to explain the movie to everyone we watched it with (they did not have Four Lokos, they were sober) because even they had no idea what was going on, and there were a bunch of unexplained scenes that you can only understand if you read the book. For example they’ll flash a scene with Anya Taylor Joy and you’re gonna be like wtf, but since we had a guide he told us that’s his sister and his moms race can see shit or something? Idk, I don’t remember but I think you get the point. Luckily he was our guide. You need to watch this movie with a guide or you’re just gonna be watching people hanging out in the sand. However I do not think this movie is bad, it’s well made. Very visually interesting despite the fact that it’s just sand, and the characters are interesting, the mystery is interesting. It’s also not poorly paced, it just felt slow for my taste. What brings it down to a 2 is that you basically either have to read the books or watch a YouTube video to understand what’s going on and in my opinion that is a film that doesn’t do its job well. If you can’t understand the story from watching the movie then it failed. I believe it has failed a bit as a film, but it’s quality saves it hence the slightly below average rating. TLDR: Watch it off of 2 Four Lokos because you’re not gonna understand what’s going on anyways.

Dune annoyed me during this viewing, and it falls off each time I watch it. Let's call this the " Endgame paradigm", and blame my excising liberalism. I'd like to make three points, or point out three categories which I see as quite deficient. Firstly: Fremen Denis elects for a blankly Afro-Asiatic look for the Fremen, making them a simultaneously sub-Saharan, Middle-eastern, and North African people. Nevermind that they have been an isolated population with nye-on zero outside inter-mingling possible. He also chooses to include death wailing in the grieving of Jamis. This genero-ethnic mix betrays the desire to vaguely represent all of the (virtuous) third world in the Fremen, and to marry this minted people with Islam. It berays the portrayal into a more favourable framing than that of Frank Herbert, and complicates the story with a more cosmopolitan, pluralist appearance than was given them by their creator. Denis wants the residents of Arrakis to be somewhat blameless in their behaviour and sympathetic in their desires, even if they are implied to be stupid by following Paul. Yes, this is a backwards culture, but it is one that Denis seems to simultaneously revere and chide. This is a problem for many modern liberals, who would love to totally embrace Islam and Islamists, but can’t quite get over their pesky superstition. Attila and the witch doctor. Second: Method As has become an assumption of modern production, handheld, mid-close shots with a shallow depth-of-field obfuscate the production elements in the background. The reflecting pool with Stilgar and Jessica is a good example. What is the point of all of the beautiful and very detailed work of set production if we cannot see it? This method also subverts the style of the sci-fi/warfare epic we know - work of the likes of David Lean - which is a fine stylistic choice in a vacuum, surely, but aggravating when it seems to genuinely lessen the feature. Where are our grand wide shots in 65mm? They disappeared by taste, and have not returned because of our self-importance and our view of method as a continuum from which we would be foolish to get off. As a result, I dislike much of how the film was shot. Opening with such a stylized eclipse scene does the rest of the film no favours. "Realism" apparently means no lighting or blocking work in most shots. That might also have something to do with the fact that most shots are CG, or contain CG composites. The very effective scenes (like hunting Harkonnen in the sandstorm ) make you wonder how much more effective they might have been with better lighting. And there are tons of lens flares here like would get Zach Snyder made fun of, but I have heard nothing of them. So I don't think I like Greig Fraser. Third: Meaning The movie thematically leans deeper into the commentary and critique of the novel, and does so inelegantly. With every modern auteur who claims themselves a "realist" whose joy it is to approximate reality, there is this kind of inelegance and incoherency which pervades their films. (For example: in fidelity to the faith, all Hollywood productions are now pluralist and cosmopolitan after the manner of the creators' experience walking down the street, regardless of their diegetic setting.) Despite Frank Herbert’s principal antagonist in this analogy, Dune the Movie's religious critique is more directed at Christianity than it is Islam. The local religion of the Arrakeans (more analogous of Islam, and more sympathetic) is subservient to the misanthropic political calculation of the Bene Gesserit, who themselves firmly believe in a messiah figure, but one of their own making; they believe that they can conjure his coming. Ultimately, his arrival is so great and terrible as none of them could have foreseen, and though the religious leaders are put off of his upending and (yet) fulfilling their prophecy, they are eventually powerless to do anything about the rise of the faith of Lisan al Ga'ib, or of the number of his adherents. We the audience are given an anachronism in Chani and the disbelieving secularists for our point-of-view character, and Denis ensures that they make all the right assertions. Excepting, of course, that assertive question or two which could cause Paul pause... From whence are these dreams coming? Obviously, the story parallels better with the advent of Christ to the upheaval of the Jewish legalists and fulfillment of their prophecy, and so this portion of the film plays a bit like historical fan fiction, wherein the atheist of today gets to go back and ask his brilliant and cutting questions of Jesus of Nazareth. He, of course, can see right through the religious deception. From all of this modernist compulsion to the "realism" of our day, and a compunction against representing women, minorities, or, indeed, rational (unreligious) people badly (or at least, without excusing them by trauma or manipulation from their bad behaviour), the film's immersion strains. The anachronism of a complete lack of belief from Chani and the secularists is one of the first inflection points. (The secular Fremen are a somewhat large and vocal number in the film, enough to make the distinction of the "southern fundamentalists" a relevant one, even if not subtle.) Chani will talk both in the novel and these movies as a believer of something. Across the mediums, one can hear her - say that Shai-hulud is sacred, especially in his role in the production of spice, - assert that water and the burial rites are important in a spiritual, and not just practical sense, - say that spice is her people's birthright, and - talk of her son, and of her husband's prodigious sister providentially (as though some force brought each to them). Chani's assassination in this film (a wholly different character than the novel, and self-contradictory in the movies themselves) happens to bring her from adapted character, to one with the same thoroughly modern opinion of religion as the writers. Imagine that. And so, with this self-portrait of Denis, we are left to conclude that more than an audience-insert with whom we are meant to sympathize (and by whom we transpose ourselves into the story), Chani is intended as a theme and message delivering bullhorn -- a manner by which the writers might tell you what the story is about. Which is how we get lines like, "You wanna control people? You tell them a messiah will come, then they wait for centuries." More than just a thematic narrator, she is the writer’s holy self-insert, for where Paul is in agreement with Chani, deriving his understanding of the world through her, he is in the right. Only when he begins to reject her framing, making use of his power and of the religious fervour of the Fremen, does he begin to be wrong. "What your people did to this world is heartbreaking." - "We gave them something to hope for." - "That's not hope!" contrasted with “I am pointing the way! (…) God be my witness: I am the Lisan al-Gaib. I will lead you to paradise!” In Denis’ movie, a character's proximity to the masculine political tendencies (exercising direct authority, reacting aggressively when faced with hostility, viewing war as a political solution, et al.), and, more crucially, their proximity to the religious determines their quality. The feminist and anti-Christian sentiment in the film was inevitable, the outworking of Herbert’s own framing, and of Denis and the writers writing what they know: they weigh every (white) man, colonial effort, and every Christian, and find them wanting. It makes their job easier that conflating these is something that we already do, as history’s colonial efforts were often white and Christian. And Herbert gives the modern creator many excuses for woman worship in particular. Setting quite the bar for inelegance already, the Chani character being made a cudgel for the writer to beat the viewer about the ears with the right interpretation of things is somehow not an assassination so severe as that of Stilgar. His character turned into a joke as he was is not appropriate to the tone, nor useful to the theme. In so doing, the writers sabotage his contributions to Paul's own "conversion" to his myth. It takes the teeth out of the line, "I don't care what you believe! I believe!" if we are constantly jeering at the silliness of faith. A driving component of Frank Herbert’s work was to show the signs and wonders of Paul as a genuinely compelling, insidious deception. Gawking at the silliness of faith and prophecy constantly does not help us to find the myth compelling, especially when the character who is meant to represent sincere faith to us as a cautionary warning is the one at whom we have been laughing. Additionally, Denis in his secular modernism cannot resist giving everything a science-y explanation, leaving nothing but the visions to the spiritual, with even those receiving a handwave as, "planted by the Bene Gesserit." (That is the best explanation as given by the book, near as I can remember, but the impression is given in the film that it is some kind of device – whether psychological or technological – that has achieved this, and that this inception is not even done by a spiritual means. Meaning that the Bene Gesserit have a closer relation in Villeneuve to Scientology and hypnotists than they do any of the Christian tradition.) The mystery of the spiritual force at work in the events of this universe is part of the compelling nature of the narrative. Who or what force is at work in these events? Is this messiah who can see the future really possible, and is it really Paul? Even if we rug-pull all of the spiritual elements at the last minute for the big reveal that it was the Order all along, there would be a more convincing conniving and malevolent quality to Paul’s works, which better sells the theme. We are meant to come away from this tale feeling cautiously inward, wondering where we have been the victim of religious propaganda, or how we might have been carried off by soaring rhetoric and religious zealotry. Did anyone walk away from the movie Dune: Part Two thinking that they had seen a serious critique of religion? Did anyone walk out with that worry that they too would have been swept up in Paul’s ascendency if they were one of the Fremen? In all the confusing rhetoric of the film, the point is that you, audience member, would have something to latch on to. The strategy is shotgun vagary: there’s something in it for everyone. Just as the casting means there's someone in it for everyone. With the first Dune , I had a hope that there was a resurgence of questions about faith and fate in film. Blade Runner 's moral clarity made me even more hopeful as to Villeneuve's chances with Paul. Unfortunately, he is evidently still an atheist. Dune: Part Two is, however (as I often caveat movies, and for your sake, dear reader), in portions, very fun to watch. While I have more to say about the technique of the film, I have probably reached your limit, haven't I? I know I have reached my own. 50/100

(Written in 2026) So, after 2 years of reflection (more like 10 months but shhhh), I've come to the realization that Dune: Part Two is overrated. This film contains very little of what I enjoyed about the first film, and it's so generally unimpressive that its flimsy narrative takes center stage. Gone are the complex politics of Dune and its varied and complex scenery, insert a rehash of the already lackluster score of the first film, and a lack of technical flair from every department, and you get this film. The cast is fine, although generally weaker than in the first film. The cinematography and sound are still good (although less impressive than Dune ), but the production design is too bland, and Fraser's insistence on using mostly wide/extra wide shots showing mostly empty scenery doesn't hide the production design flaws. The editing is also notably worse here, Denis Villeneuve/Joe Walker remain insistent to linger on certain shots for too long, once again grinding the pace to a complete halt, and wringing out whatever energy the viewer has left. Back to the cast, Austin Butler is a very disappointing Feyd-Rautha. He does a uniquely awful job at instilling fear (what with his on-again/off-again Elvis accent ruining whatever was left of the dialogue), which betrays the work he put in on the combat choreography. He also lacks any real skill physicality-wise, all of the random yells, spasms, and "quirks" of his performance come off as comedic and are totally unfit for the character's role in the film. The action sequences in the film are also no longer the strength they were in the first film, with Villeneuve's staging and Frasier's cinematography becoming progressively less interesting throughout the film.

Visuellement bluffant, émotionnellement creux. Aie Aie Aie. Je m'attendais à BEAUCOUP mieux que la partie 1, mais à peine. Toutefois, les raisons de mon retrait sont différentes entre la partie 1 et la partie 2. À de nombreuses reprises, j'ai trouvé le film austère et glacial avec un manque de liens émotionnels avec les personnages. Par exemple, j'aurais aimé voir comment Chani et Paul se sont rapprochés car au départ elle avait quand même des doutes et lui avait ses visions prémonitoires la concernant. Enfaite, j'ai trouvé leur rapprochement hyper soudain comme précipité tout en étant assumé et c'est pas pour moi. De manière générale, je sens une certaine précipitation des évènements de la part de Villeneuve, ce qui m'a fait décroché. Des années ont l'air de passer comme des semaines là où, je peux le sentir, les livres doivent probablement bien nous le faire sentir ce temps qui passe. Autre remarque, l'expansion et la croissance de la "religion" de la mère de Paul qui est fourré au 1000e plan du film. J'aurais aimé un focus dessus parce qu'une parole de la mère qui dit "il faut commencer par ceux qui ont peurs" et puis "on a fini avec le nord, passons au sud"... mouais Denis steuplait hein. Des révélations chocs comme le fait que la mère de Paul soit la fille du baron et la mort symbolique de celui-ci part la main de son petit-fils m'ont laissé de marbre. Je soupçonne que cela s'explique par, pour moi encore une fois, un retrait de l'intrigue politique au second plan afin de polluer le premier plan du film sur le fait que tout indique que Paul est le Lisan Al-Ghaib (jeu de mot qui m'a fait croire à autre chose et je pense que c'était totalement le but). Je ne dis pas qu'il n'y a aucune intrigue politique, ce serait mentir sans vergogne. Je dis plutôt que sa place est hybride là où elle devrait être centrale. Toutefois, je comprendrais que d'autres ne pensent la même chose, et c'est OK. On retrouve des personnages qui se veulent être impactant retirer de tout leur éclat dû à un manque de place affligeant (ex: Empereur, Rautha). J'ai également du mal à croire en la relation entre Paul et sa mère. Leurs interactions me font plus penser à un frère et sa soeur plutôt qu'à un fils et sa mère. Vers la fin elle se reprend mais bon. Si on recentre notre attention sur Paul, j'ai pas compris en quoi c'était évident qu'il aille chercher la potion bleue. Pour moi c'est un peu sorti de nulle part. Oui oui sa prescience etc mais je suis pas convaincu par ce que je vois, justement parce que tout va vite et de manière très déconnecté. Et son shift ne s'explique pas tant que ça, on peut le comprendre en l'imaginant mais ce n'est jamais rien de factuel là où on comprenait celui d'Anakin par exemple. D'ailleurs, on sent que ce film est un film qui prépare le prochain. Ça m'a un peu dérangé. mais ça reste minime. Passons au positif, c'est déprimant sinon. J'ai beaucoup aimé le choix visuel de passer de la couleur au noir et blanc dans l'arène. Je n'ai pas d'explication au phénomène mais c'était sympa. De plus, les éléments du film sont présents mais mal intégré à mon avis, c'est dommage. (pff j'étais censé virer au positif) L'amourette bien que rapide est mignonne. On peut imaginer que Paul et Chani tienne énormément l'un à l'autre. De plus, j'ai bien aimé la première traversée du désert de Paul avec Chani. Les plans étaient beaux, l'ambiance était chic, les chorégraphies étaient apaisantes par leur synchronicité. Bref c'était chouette. Enfin, j'aime bien l'idée d'un faux saveur qui s'approprie les mythes pour parvenir à ses fins. C'est intéressant. On en vient même à se demander si le mythe est réellement faux ou s'il est devenu réel à force de le propager ou s'il a toujours été réel. Notre avis peut néanmoins se trouver biaisé par la mise en scène et le pdv de Paul (visions etc). Bref, c'est sympa ça. PS: Voir les idées des adaptations m'a donné envie de débuter les livres un jour. J'pense que j'apprécierai plus. Ou bien pas du tout et ça conclura ma tentative désespérée :( PS2: Niveau religion, et ce que traduit cette oeuvre, je préfère me taire sinon j'vais écrire 3 pavés supplémentaires. Pas content. Frank Herbert est un cas mais Denis Villeneuve est tout aussi en faute pour l'image qu'il renvoie. PS3: Je pense sincèrement qu'une série aurait été plus adaptée pour cette oeuvre.

Dune 2; Harkonnen Boogaloo The production on these movies continues to blow me away.  It feels like watching something from Moebius or Druillet in live action.  The costumes, the music, the differences in the worlds, heck even the language is all so well done that it feels both alien and completely natural all at the same time. I also really loved the looks of all of the Harkonnen machines.  One of the things that Villeneuve and the crew here have done very well across both films is give a sense of the weight and physics of these things.  The giant worms, the miners, the crashed ornithopters.  They all have very believable weight to them.  I've seen several bad sci-fi films where they forget about that in the fx.  They'll have these giant machines that look like they are walking across rice paper without damaging it. Watching these movies gives me the same sort of feeling that I got when I was watching The Lord of the Rings for the first time.

Denis Villeneuve en su máximo esplendor. La película es una obra maestra. Realmente magistral. Es de esas películas en las que cuesta encontrar algo que no esté a la altura: el guion, la dirección, la fotografía, los efectos visuales, las actuaciones y, por supuesto, la apoteósica banda sonora de Hans Zimmer. Absolutamente todo funciona. La primera vez que la vi en el cine, en IMAX, salí completamente alucinado. La amé de principio a fin. Pero después de haber leído Dune, la experiencia fue todavía mejor. Amé el libro de Frank Herbert y, precisamente por eso, una de las cosas que más me impresionó de la primera película fue su enorme fidelidad a la obra original. Sin embargo, al leer el libro y volver a Dune: Part Two, entendí que Denis Villeneuve tomó muchas más libertades para llevar la historia hacia una dirección diferente. Y, lejos de molestarme, me pareció maravilloso. Porque eso demuestra que Villeneuve no buscó simplemente trasladar el libro página por página a la pantalla. Entendió su esencia, tomó decisiones propias y construyó su propia visión de Dune. Y eso, para mí, es precisamente lo que hacen los grandes directores. Volver a ver esta película una y otra vez es un verdadero lujo. Cada visionado permite apreciar algo nuevo: la composición de cada plano, los colores, la fotografía, los detalles de los escenarios, la magnitud de Arrakis y el nivel técnico de una producción que visualmente es simplemente impresionante. Y si hablamos de sus grandes virtudes, es imposible no detenerse en la banda sonora de Hans Zimmer. Personalmente, es mi compositor favorito de música para cine y aquí vuelve a entregar un trabajo extraordinario, completamente diferente al de la primera película. Hay momentos en los que basta con cerrar los ojos para sentir el desierto de Arrakis, la inmensidad del planeta y, sobre todo, cómo la tensión va aumentando poco a poco hasta convertir la historia en la promesa de una guerra santa. Las actuaciones también están a un nivel extraordinario. Era algo que podía esperarse después de una primera película con un elenco tan sólido, pero las nuevas incorporaciones elevan todavía más el conjunto. Austin Butler como Feyd-Rautha y Florence Pugh como Irulan son excelentes, pero para mí hay dos que se roban absolutamente la película: Javier Bardem como Stilgar y Timothée Chalamet como Paul Atreides. Chalamet, especialmente, entrega una de las mejores actuaciones de su carrera. Se puede ver en su rostro el tormento, el miedo y el dolor de un hombre que sabe perfectamente hacia dónde lo está llevando el camino que ha elegido, pero que también entiende que cada paso que da puede acercarlo cada vez más al caos que intentaba evitar. Dune: Part Two es una película maravillosa, épica y técnicamente impresionante. Una obra que consiguió conquistar tanto al público como a la crítica y que, en mi opinión, tiene absolutamente merecidos todos los elogios que recibió. Denis Villeneuve tomó una de las obras más importantes de la ciencia ficción, la llevó a la pantalla grande con una visión propia y consiguió convertirla en una experiencia cinematográfica monumental. Una verdadera obra de arte moderna.

Sé que la calificación puede generar preguntas pero afortunadamente tengo bastante que decir de la que me parece una de las películas más sobrevaloradas de la historia. Vi la primer película en su momento y me pareció interesante pero nada espectacular, destacaba en el elenco y en los visuales pero nada que me llevaría a repetirla. Esa película planteó la adaptación un universo el cual pude ver que tiene como eje central la política, el problema de hacer historias sobre política es que se debe tratar con extrema atención el diálogo y el conflicto en cuestión, pues si ninguno de los dos puntos es interesante, no genera un gancho para ver horas de discusiones con el motivo de llevar un conflicto a una resolución contundente. En su momento no tomé tan en cuenta eso al ser solo la primera parte de Dune, pero cuando ves la segunda parte de esa historia sabiendo que es ya la mitad de una trilogía y el interés se siente vacío, ya es preocupante. Cuando Dune parte 2 salió vi gente alabándola como una de las mejores sino que la mejor experiencia cinematográfica de los últimos años, no podría estar más en desacuerdo y sostengo mi punto en base a su carencia de identidad. Es bien sabido que Star Wars plagió en muchos aspectos (aunque sean mínimos) a los libros de Dune, sin embargo, el reconocimiento a Star Wars viene de cómo a pesar de ello se logró crear un universo con identidad, el cual no viene de una obra previa sino que directamente nació en el cine, siendo que ahora su mundo es identificable al igual que sus personajes e historias, ya es un icono de la cultura pop. Ahora parece que los papeles se han invertido y Dune que en teoría es “la obra original” pareciera que quiere replicar a Star Wars, lo cual tiene sentido, la adaptación original de Dune fue un total fracaso. Dune parte 2 no parece que haga un trabajo por sacar a relucir su concepto y su mundo, más bien parece que quiere replicar lo que su supuesta copia “la venganza de los Sith” hizo años atrás para ser el éxito que fue y es lamentable pensar como la franquicia que en teoría es la copia me parece que tiene mucha más identidad que la obra original. No me quedo con los ambientes ni escenarios de la película, no me quedo con los nombres de los personajes, el conflicto no tiene lo suyo, solo parece que quieren convertir a Paul Atreides en otro Anakin Skywalker en vez de darle valor por ser su propio personaje. Y no, no es mala película, la disfrute, me emocione, estuve atento a ella y es una mejora absoluta de la 1 en todo aspecto, principalmente en el ritmo. Pero me parece desmedido el escándalo que en su momento se hizo al nombrar Dune Parte 2 como una de las mejores películas de la historia cuando me parece una buena película más del montón que destaca únicamente por su alto presupuesto. Personalmente tampoco siento que el elenco haya dado su mejor trabajo, sentí que igual hubo un hype desmedido por varios personajes y actores que tampoco son la gran cosa. Mi conclusión es que venimos de tantas películas malas que una película decente pareció una obra maestra a los ojos de todos, porque de lo contrario no me explico el hype.

Villeneuve‘s Chani continues to baffle me. Whilst I’m glad he gives her character a larger more independent role, her actions as a whole (movie-wise) still doesn’t make a lot of sense: Paul tells her about his nightmares of the genocide of billions in his name, repeatedly refuses to go south in order to avoid said fate, but is required to do so, so he can ensure the security of the Fremen and their control of Arrakis/Dune. Without this, there would be no Fremen left to retake Dune as she believes it to be carried out. What I do find completely understandable is being extremely pissed off that your partner proposes to another woman right in front of you. Besides that, she really is being ridiculous in her actions despite disagreeing with the methods. Again, I have to mention how much of a miscast Walken feels as Emperor, although he is not as prominent in Messiah, his character is incredibly weak and pathetic (in this movie) compared to the young, prideful, flamboyant, and calculated person he is in the book. Hopefully Part 3 explains these ‘problems’ I have away and ties the saga up neatly.

Wow wow wow - genuinely epic in every sense of the word. The cinematography is just outstanding, the score is spine-tingling, the performances are smashed out the park; this is proper cinema. I’d say this is a ‘generational’ film if that term wasn’t so overused, to the point where your coworker uses it when they have a half-decent iced latte, therefore ruining the words you can actually use to describe this level of greatness. It’s not perfect - the ending feels rushed and at times the pacing is so fast it feels like an overcorrection to the criticisms of how slow Dune One was. Christopher Walken is badly cast in this (it’s just Christopher Walken in Dune as opposed to The Emperor), Zendaya’s arc is rushed with both how quickly she falls in AND out of love with Paul. Still, I watch films hoping there are epic action sequences, compelling dialogue, interesting character arcs & full of good shots/cinematography - this has all of those in abundance. It’s not a perfect movie, but it’s a perfect film for my tastes. Cannot wait for Dune Three.
